parole.significato: Used in systematic names for many chemical compounds, including compounds containing only two elements
parole.testo: From Latin -idus. 3 meaning is from Ancient Greek -ειδής (-eidḗs)
From New Latin -ītis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis).

parole.significato: abbot (superior or head of an abbey or monastery)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin abbas, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”).

parole.significato: accent (stress or a pitch in articulation)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin accentus, a calque of Ancient Greek προσῳδία (prosōidía, “prosody, accent”).
From New Latin Agave, from Ancient Greek Ἀγαυή (Agauḗ), name of one of the daughters of Cadmus, from ἀγαυός (agauós, “noble, illustrious”).
From Latin alabaster, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros), from earlier ἀλάβαστος (alábastos)
From Latin amphibium (neuter of amphibius), from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιον (amphíbion), neuter of ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφί (amphí, “both”) and βίος (bíos, “life”).
From Latin ammoniacum, from Ancient Greek ἀμμωνιακόν (ammōniakón).
Via Latin analyticus from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós), derived from ἀνάλυσις (análusis)
From Latin antithesis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), equivalent to anti- + tese.
From New Latin apnoea, from Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia).

parole.significato: pharmacy (a place where prescription drugs are dispensed)
parole.testo: From Latin apotheca (“storehouse”), from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of butik (“shop”) (via French) and bodega (“bar”) (via Spanish).
From Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).
From Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, “town hall”).
From Latin arteria, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría).
Via Latin asparagus from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
Ultimately from Latin asteriscus.
From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βᾰ́σῐς (bắsĭs). Doublet of base, and also related to komme, from the same ultimate source.
From Danish beryl + -ium, from Latin beryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos).

parole.significato: Bible (Christian or Jewish holy book; also used figuratively)
parole.testo: From Latin biblia (“Christian scripture”), from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”).
Learned borrowing from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point, goad, sting”).
Borrowed from Latin cithara (or through another intermediate language), from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “kind of harp”).
From New Latin cyclus, from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).
From Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros).
From Late Latin cystis, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis).
Ultimately from Latin diagnōsis, from Ancient Greek διάγνωσις (diágnōsis).
From Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos). Doublet of degn.
Via Latin dialectus from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος (diálektos, “conversation, way of speaking”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to discuss”), from διά (diá, “through”) + λέγω (légō, “to speak”).
From Medieval Latin diamans, probably from metathesis of Late Latin adimas, from Latin adamās, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas).
From Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”).
From Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēccō, later variant of ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ).
Via Latin elephantus from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās); replaced Old Danish fil (“elephant”), Old Norse fíll (cf. older Danish filsben (“ivory”)).
From Latin electrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).
empiri + -iker, from Latin empiricus, derived from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρικός (empeirikós).
From Latin encyclopaedia, from Ancient Greek ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία (enkúklios paideía, “the circle of arts and sciences, curriculum”).
From Late Latin epidemia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδημία (epidēmía).
From Latin epilēpticus, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληπτικός (epilēptikós).

parole.significato: epistle; a literary composition in the form of a letter
parole.testo: From Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ). Compare Old Norse pistill.
evangelie + -isk, from Latin evangelicus, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελικός (euangelikós).

parole.significato: evangelist; a preacher of the gospel
parole.testo: From Latin ēvangelista, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs). Equivalent to evangelie + -ist.
From Late Latin pharaō, from Ancient Greek φαραώ (pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“palace, pharaoh”), literally pr (“house”) + ꜥꜣ (“great, big”).
Via Latin philosophicus, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφικός (philosophikós). Equivalent to filosofi + -isk.
From Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon).
From Latin phoenix, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix). Compare Swedish fenix, Icelandic fönix.

parole.significato: a geranium, plant of genus Geranium
parole.testo: From New Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γέρανος (géranos, “crane”).
From Old Danish gryph, from Latin grȳphus, from Ancient Greek γρύψ (grúps). Doublet of grib and kerub. Compare Old Norse gripr, Old Swedish griper, Swedish grip.

parole.significato: rubber (pliable material derived from the sap of the rubber tree)
parole.testo: From Old Danish gumi, borrowed from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).
From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”).
Medieval Latin, from Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon”).
From Latin historia (“history, story”), from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, “inquiry, history”).
From Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon).
Via Late Latin idyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion).
Via Latin idēa from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), derived from the verb ἰδεῖν (ideîn, “to see”). Compare also English idea.

parole.significato: fireplace, hearth (in an open recess in the wall of a room)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caminus, from Ancient Greek κάμινος (káminos).
From Latin camera (“room, chamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vault”). Doublet of kamera.
From Latin capparis, from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis, “caper”).
From Latin catapulta, from Ancient Greek καταπέλτης (katapéltēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κᾰτᾰ́ρροος (kătắrrhoos).
From Latin cataracta, from Ancient Greek καταρράκτης (katarrháktēs).
From New Latin catharticus, from Ancient Greek καθαρτικός (kathartikós). Equivalent to katarsis + -sk.
From Latin cathedrālis, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).
From Latin cholericus, from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ, “bile, gall”).

parole.significato: chord; straight line connecting points in a circle's circumference, sometimes excluding the diameter
parole.testo: From Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).
From Old Danish kyruæl, from Latin chaerephylla, plural of chaerephyllum, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).
From Latin lēthargia, from Ancient Greek ληθαργία (lēthargía).
From Latin lethargicus, from Ancient Greek ληθαργικός (lēthargikós). Equivalent to letargi + -sk.
From Medieval Latin litania, letania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).
From Latin magīa, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
From Ecclesiastical Latin martyr from Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
From Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) and φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).
From Latin metallum, from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “metal, mine”).
From Latin methodus (“method, way of teaching”), from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, “method, fashion”). Compare French méthode and German Methode.
From metode (“method”) + -isk, from Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós, “methodical, orderly, businesslike, systematic”). Compare French méthodique and German methodisch.
From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Borrowing from Latin Maurus, from Ancient Greek μαυρός (maurós, “dark”).
Borrowed from Latin mūsēum, from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon, “a shrine of the Muses”), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
From Latin mūsica (“music”), from Ancient Greek μουσῐκή (mousĭkḗ).
From Latin mystērium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion).
From Late Latin mystica, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós).
Via Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós).
From Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos)
From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).
From Latin narcoticum, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτῐκός (narkōtĭkós).
From Latin nervus, and Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron).
From New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
from Latin Ōceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós)
From Late Latin oda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).
From Latin orgia (“orgy”), from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia, “secret rites, mysteries”).

parole.significato: orthodox (conforming to traditional or generally accepted rules or beliefs)
parole.testo: From Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos).
From Latin paragraphus, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos). Equivalent to para- + -graf.
Via Latin parallēlus from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos, “side-by-side”), from παρά (pará, “by”) + ἀλλήλοις (allḗlois, “each other”)

From Latin parallēlogrammum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon), neuter of παραλληλόγραμμος (parallēlógrammos, “limited by parallel lines”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos) + γραμμή (grammḗ).

parole.significato: parasite (a (generally undesirable) living organism that exists by stealing the resources needed by another (generally…
parole.testo: Via Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos).
From Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”).
Via Latin pelecanus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán).

From Latin peripheria, from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia, “periphery”), from περιφερής (peripherḗs, “moving around, round, circular”), from περιφέρω (periphérō, “to carry around, move around”), from περί (perí, “around, about, near”) and φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: pirate (a criminal who plunders at sea)
parole.testo: From Latin pīrāta (“pirate”), from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs, “pirate”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).
From Latin polyhistor, from Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr).

parole.significato: pore (a tiny opening in the skin)
parole.testo: From Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros).
From Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma).
From Late Latin prophetia, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía, “prophecy”), from προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “speaker of a god”).

parole.significato: pygmy (member of one of the various tribes in Africa or Asia that are characterized by a short stature)
parole.testo: Via Latin pygmaeus from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “mythical dwarf”), derived from the noun πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist”)
Via Latin paedagōgus from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”).

From New Latin paedagōgica, a substantivization of the feminine form of the adjective paedagōgicus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós, “pertaining to teaching”), παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”) + -ικός (-ikós).
Via Latin rhetorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ).
From Latin sapphīrus (“saphire”), from Ancient Greek σάπφειρος (sáppheiros).

parole.significato: stage (platform for performing in a theatre)
parole.testo: From Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).
From Latin scēptrum, from Ancient Greek σκῆπτρον (skêptron).
From Latin sphēra, sphaera (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, globe”).

parole.significato: siren (an alarm with a piercing sound)
parole.testo: Via Latin Sīrēn from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). As a term for an “alarm” influenced by French sirène.
From Late Latin scepticus, ultimately from Ancient Greek σκεπτικός (skeptikós)
Via Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós).

parole.significato: stigma (an indication of infamy or disgrace)
parole.testo: From Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”).
Via Latin sȳcophanta, from Ancient Greek συκοφάντης (sukophántēs).
From Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”).
From Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia)

parole.significato: syndrome (recognizable pattern of symptoms or behaviours)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).
From Latin synecdoche, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ).

parole.significato: syntax (the rules governing how words are combined to form phrases and sentences in a particular language or in general)
parole.testo: Via Latin syntaxis from Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis, “arrangement, composition, syntax”).
From late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “organised whole, body”), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
From Latin talentum, from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent”).
From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología).
From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέᾱτρον (théātron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see", "to watch", "to observe”).
From Latin thesis, from Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis)
From Latin traumaticus, from Ancient Greek τραυμᾰτῐκός (traumătĭkós).
From Latin tri- (“three”) and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).
From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “fever, stupor”).

parole.significato: tyrant (a leader in many Ancient Greek city states)
parole.testo: Via Latin tyrannus from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos).

parole.significato: verb (a word that indicates an action, event, or a state)
parole.testo: From Latin verbum (“word”). In the grammatical sense, the Latin word was a semantic loan from Ancient Greek ῥῆμα (rhêma, “word, verb”).
From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”).
From Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos), equivalent to ærke- + engel.

parole.significato: ether (the substance supposed to fill the upper regions over the clouds)
parole.testo: Via Latin aethēr (“air, sky”) from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “heaven, upper air”).
From Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Equivalent to øko- + -nomi.
